newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma bomb trial jurors end day with no verdict.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma bomb trial jurors end day with no verdict.

text.p: The jury in the trial of accused Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh deliberated for a second full day on Saturday, but did not reach a verdict.

Federal Judge Richard Matsch warned the jury of seven men and five women not to discuss the case again until they resumed their deliberations on Sunday morning. They were expected to work a half day on Sunday.
"There have been no communications from the jury today," said Matsch, meaning jurors had not requested clarifications of the law or asked to have testimony read back to them.

The jurors were sifting through five weeks of testimony and hundreds of pieces of evidence presented during the trial of McVeigh, who has been charged with blowing up the Alfred P. Murrah federal building on April 19, 1995, killing 168 people.
McVeigh's chief attorney Stephen Jones said his client was feeling well. "He was fine. I visited with him for a few minutes and he was in good spirits," Jones said.
When asked what he made of the jury's continuing deliberations, Jones said: "I don't read tea leaves."
One relative of a bombing victim fainted outside the courthouse and had to be helped away.
In court McVeigh smiled nervously before the jury was brought out and later talked animatedly with his attorneys.
The wait for a verdict was starting to take its toll on relatives of bombing victims, many of whom had hoped for a quick guilty verdict.
Some were doing crossword puzzles in a nearby church as they waited for the verdict.

"We're all on pins and needles. It's like a humongous rollercoaster. One minute you'll be laughing, the next minute you'll be crying. It hurts. We just couldn't perceive they would be taking this long," said Dan McKinney, whose wife Linda, 47, died in the bombing.

But Sharon Medearis, whose husband Claude, a U.S. Customs Service agent, died in the blast, remained patient. "It would be nice to get a verdict but they are trying to decide the fate of a man, and I think It's going to take a while," she said in Oklahoma City.
Denver attorney Andrew Cohen, who has been monitoring the trial, said he did not read anything into the length of deliberations because the jury had a lot of evidence to assess.
There was no indication how long the jury would take to reach a verdict.

If McVeigh is convicted, a second phase will be held to determine whether he is to be sentenced to life in prison or death. Asked if he were preparing for the so-called penalty phase, Jones would only say he was preparing for all eventualities.
Several hundred journalists kept watch at the federal courthouse in Denver, which was ringed by tight security as it has been throughout the high-profile trial.
McVeigh, 29, pleaded not guilty to charges of conspiracy, bombing and first-degree murder of the eight federal agents killed in the blast.

The prosecution portrayed McVeigh as a right-wing fanatic driven to carry out the bombing by hatred of the government, his anger fuelled by the way federal agents handled a siege at the Branch Davidian compound in Waco, Texas, in 1993.

The defence argued that authorities arrested the wrong man. The defence team tried to discredit key prosecution witnesses, attack the reliability of the government's scientific evidence and undermine eyewitnesses who identified McVeigh as the man who rented a truck the government says was used in the bombing.
The jury heard from 137 prosecution and 25 defence witnesses.
The jurors were not allowed to take notes during the trial, but evidence was set up in an auxiliary courtroom so they could view it.
